findings.title: Google credential key is overwritten with the zod SafeParse wrapper object on every refresh
findings.body: `parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns the raw `safeParse` result (`{ success: true, data: {...} }`), not the parsed data. The previous code stored `googleCredentialSchema.parse(googleCredentials)` (the token object). Now `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })` writes `{success, data}` into `credential.key`, so on the next instantiation `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` fails and the Google Calendar integration breaks for that user. This happens for every token refresh regardless of whether credential syncing is enabled, i.e. it corrupts all Google Calendar credentials in production.

findings.title: minimumTokenResponseSchema is malformed; computed keys evaluate to "[object Object]" and all other fields are stripped
findings.body: `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` both evaluate to the string "[object Object]", so the schema is effectively `{ access_token: string, "[object Object]": unknown }`. Zod objects strip unknown keys by default, so when credential sync is enabled every parsed response only contains `access_token`; `expires_in`/`expiry_date` etc. are dropped. Callers then compute `Date.now() + undefined * 1000` (NaN expiry in Zoom) or lose the expiry entirely (Office365), causing the token to be considered expired/invalid on every call. The intent ('any numeric property is the expiry', 'allow other properties') cannot be expressed this way; use `.passthrough()` or an explicit schema.

findings.title: Missing refresh_token is replaced with literal placeholder "refresh_token", which then overwrites the real refresh token in DB
findings.body: When the refresh response lacks `refresh_token`, the function injects the string `"refresh_token"` into `data`. Callers spread this data over the stored credential (`o365AuthCredentials = {...o365AuthCredentials, ...tokenResponse.data}` in office365calendar, `key.refresh_token = newTokens.refresh_token` in zoomvideo), so the genuine refresh token is destroyed and replaced by a bogus string. Microsoft legitimately omits `refresh_token` on some refresh responses (the schema marks it optional), so this corrupts Office 365 credentials even with credential sync disabled, and permanently breaks the credential once the access token expires.

findings.title: `prisma` is used but never imported
findings.body: `await prisma.credential.update(...)` references `prisma`, but there is no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"` in this file. This is a type-check failure and, at runtime, a ReferenceError that makes every Salesforce CalendarService instantiation reject, breaking the Salesforce integration entirely.

findings.title: Salesforce refreshes the token unconditionally on every construction and never uses the new access token
findings.body: `getClient` now performs a refresh_token grant every time the service is constructed (no expiry check), adding an extra Salesforce API call per booking/availability check and risking rate limits. The refreshed `access_token` is stored in DB but the `jsforce.Connection` is still built with the old `credentialKey.access_token`. Additionally `response.statusText !== "OK"` is unreliable (statusText is empty on HTTP/2), so valid responses may be rejected with a 400. The refresh also bypasses `refreshOAuthTokens`, so credential syncing (the point of this PR) is not applied to Salesforce.

findings.title: Sync path returns a fetch Response regardless of what the wrapped refreshFunction would have returned
findings.body: When syncing is enabled the helper returns a raw `fetch` `Response`, but several callers expect the shape of their own refresh client: hubspot expects a `HubspotToken` object (`hubspotRefreshToken.expiresIn` → NaN expiry, `accessToken` undefined), zohocrm and zoho-bigin expect an axios response (`tokenInfo.data` is undefined → TypeError), googlecalendar expects `{ res: { data } }` (`res?.data` undefined → TypeError). So enabling `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` breaks token refresh for HubSpot, Zoho CRM, Zoho Bigin and Google Calendar. The helper needs to normalise the response (e.g. return parsed JSON) and callers must consume it consistently.

findings.title: credentialId passed where userId is expected
findings.body: `refreshOAuthTokens(..., "zoho-bigin", credentialId)` passes the credential id as the `userId` parameter. When sync is enabled the self-hoster's endpoint receives `calcomUserId=<credential id>`, so it will look up or return tokens for the wrong user (or fail). Should be `credential.userId`.

findings.title: appStoreMetadata is keyed by app directory name, not slug, so lookups by slug fail for many apps
findings.body: `appStoreMetadata[app.slug]` indexes the metadata map using the DB slug (e.g. `google-calendar`, `zoom`, `office365-calendar`), but `appStoreMetadata` is keyed by directory name (`googlecalendar`, `zoomvideo`, `office365calendar`). For every app whose dirName differs from its slug the webhook returns 404 'App not found. Ensure that you have the correct app slug', so credentials for the most common apps cannot be synced. Look up by `Object.values(appStoreMetadata).find(m => m.slug === app.slug)` instead. The same slug/dirName confusion appears in callers of `refreshOAuthTokens` (`"zoomvideo"` vs `"google-calendar"` vs `"msteams"`), making the `appSlug` sent to the sync endpoint inconsistent.

findings.title: Webhook secret compared with non-constant-time `!==` and no HTTP method restriction
findings.body: The shared secret is checked with a plain string comparison, which leaks timing information and allows byte-by-byte guessing of the secret. Use `crypto.timingSafeEqual` on equal-length buffers. The handler also accepts any HTTP method (GET included) and does not guard against `req.headers[...]` being an array. Given this endpoint writes arbitrary third-party credentials for any user id, authentication should be hardened.

findings.title: Schema parse, decryption and JSON.parse errors are uncaught and surface as 500s
findings.body: `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse`, `symmetricDecrypt` (wrong key / malformed ciphertext) and `JSON.parse` all throw synchronously and are not caught, so malformed webhook payloads produce an unhandled 500 with a stack trace instead of a 400 with a clear message. Use `safeParse` and wrap decryption in try/catch.

findings.title: Refresh failure now throws instead of logging and continuing; error details are lost
findings.body: Previously a failed parse of Microsoft's token response was logged (zod error plus raw MS response) and execution continued. Now `parseRefreshTokenResponse` throws a generic 'Invalid refreshed tokens were returned' with no detail, and the surrounding `getToken` has no catch, so the failure propagates to callers (availability/booking) and debugging information about why MS rejected the refresh is gone.
